correctness.rationale: The map Ux=((m+1)^(−1)∑_{j≤m}x_j)_m is an onto isometry from σ∞ to ℓ∞ with inverse x_m=(m+1)y_m−m y_(m−1). Conjugate unilateral convolution shift W has weights m/(m+1); W−S is compact as weights differences →0. For a∈ℓ1, f_a(W)−f_a(S) compact by ℓ1 operator convergence. At arbitrarily late disjoint blocks with phase conjugates of a_k, 0≤k≤N, the main coordinate has amplitude ≥(A−N A/(m+1)−2τ_N)||c||∞ with τ_N=∑k>N|a_k|, producing an isometric closed ℓ∞ copy on which T_a is almost A-below. This gives exact norm A, all finite Bernstein/approximation/Gelfand numbers A, and distances A to strictly singular/compact ideals. Factor analytic Wiener f_a−λ for λ∉f_a(T) into finitely many disk zero factors and an invertible analytic-Wiener factor; S−αI Fredholm of index −1 inside disk, invertible outside. Thus index=−number of interior zeros; compact equivalence transfers it to σ∞. For λ∈f_a(T), disjoint slowly tapered approximate characters are weakly null in ℓ∞, unit norm and asymptotically annihilated by f_a(S)−λ; Atkinson compact-parametrix contradiction excludes Fredholmness. Zero and scalar symbols included. The finite 1.699100899 versus 1.7 illustration is not used as proof.

Its complete HTML Sections 2–5 discuss structure and fine spectrum, but not finite s-numbers, strictly singular distances, Fredholm essential spectrum or exact index. Critically, the earlier 2026 Saha–Patra weighted-Hahn paper arXiv:2606.22912 IS NOW FULLY ACCESSIBLE in arXiv HTML, §§3–6: it establishes boundedness, a Hausdorff noncompactness compactness criterion, ordinary/fine spectrum of h_d and bs_d, but not the stated constant ideal-distance profile or Fredholm boundary for σ∞. It cannot be dismissed as unseen; full primary comparison updated. Existing general Wiener–Hopf and operator ideal theory supplies proof mechanisms, but their general theorems would need an explicit compact weighted-shift identification and sharp block lower bound in this particular nonseparable norm.

This is a complete invariant/spectral classification, not a marginal numerical improvement or reiteration of the known operator norm.
